title: Reflog and recovering lost commits
description: Learn about Reflog and recovering lost commits. Master the concepts, patterns, and best practices.

data.text: Reflog is Git's safety net. It records every update to the tip of branches and other references, making it possible to recover commits that seem lost forever.

data.title: Lesson Scope
data.text: This lesson covers reflog anatomy, recovering deleted branches, restoring lost commits, cleaning up reflog, and building team recovery workflows.

Reflog stands for reference log. Every time a branch moves, HEAD changes, or a commit is added or removed, Git records the event in a reflog. Each reference has its own reflog, and there is also a global HEAD reflog.

data.title: Viewing the Reflog
data.code: git reflog

data.title: Sample Reflog Output
data.code:
abc1234 HEAD@{0}: checkout: moving from main to feature/auth
def5678 HEAD@{1}: commit: fix(auth): add token validation
ghi9012 HEAD@{2}: rebase -i (finish): returning to refs/heads/main
jkl3456 HEAD@{3}: pull: origin main: fast-forward

data.text: Each reflog entry has a reference name, an index, the old and new SHA values, and a description of what happened. The index counts backward from the current state: HEAD@{0} is now, HEAD@{1} is the previous state.

data.title: Inspecting a Reflog Entry
data.code:
git reflog show main

# Output:
# abc1234 main@{0}: commit: feat: add dashboard
# def5678 main@{1}: rebase finished: refs/heads/main onto origin/main
# ghi9012 main@{2}: branch: created from origin/main

data.title: Reflog Is Local
data.text: Reflog lives only in your local repository. It is not shared via push or pull. If you clone a fresh copy of the repository, the reflog is empty.

If you accidentally delete a branch, its commits are not immediately gone. Git retains them as unreachable objects until garbage collection runs. Use reflog to find the tip commit and recreate the branch.

data.title: Recovering a Deleted Branch
data.code:
# Oops, deleted the branch
git branch -D feature/auth

# Find the lost commit in reflog
git reflog

# Recreate the branch at the lost commit
git branch feature-auth-recovery abc1234

data.text: If a commit is not on any branch, it is still in the repository as long as it appears in a reflog. Find the commit hash and create a new branch or cherry-pick it onto an existing branch.

data.title: Recovering a Lost Commit
data.code:
# Find the commit in reflog
git reflog | grep "lost work"

# Recover it onto a new branch
git checkout -b recovery abc1234

data.title: Garbage Collection Removes Unreachable Objects
data.text: Git periodically runs gc to prune objects that are not reachable from any branch or reflog. If you wait too long, unreachable commits may be permanently deleted.
Git reflog entries expire after 90 days by default for reachable commits and 30 days for unreachable commits. After expiration, git gc may prune the associated objects.

data.title: Reflog Expiry Configuration
data.code:
# Expire reachable entries after 90 days
git config gc.reflogExpire 90.days

# Expire unreachable entries after 30 days
git config gc.reflogExpireUnreachable 30.days

# Run garbage collection manually
git gc --prune=now

data.text: git fsck verifies the connectivity and integrity of objects in the repository. It lists dangling commits that are not referenced by any branch, which is useful when hunting for lost work outside of reflog.

data.title: Finding Dangling Commits
data.code:
git fsck --lost-found

# Output:
# dangling commit abc1234
# dangling commit def5678

data.text: git reset --hard discards working tree changes and moves the branch pointer. If you reset accidentally, the old branch tip is still in reflog. Restore it with git reset --hard HEAD@{1}.

data.title: Recovering After a Hard Reset
data.code:
# Accidentally ran
git reset --hard HEAD~3

# Recover the lost state
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}

data.title: Uncommitted Work Is Lost Forever
data.text: Reflog does not track uncommitted changes in the working tree. If you reset --hard without committing first, uncommitted work is gone. Commit or stash before dangerous operations.

A rebase that goes wrong can leave you in a detached HEAD or with lost commits. Use reflog to find the original branch position and reset to it, or use git rebase --abort if the rebase is still in progress.

data.title: Recovering from a Bad Rebase
data.code:
# Rebase broke the branch
git reflog

# Find main@{1} before the rebase
git branch -f main main@{1}

data.text: Orphaned commits exist in the object database but are not reachable from any branch, tag, or reflog entry. They are candidates for garbage collection. Use git fsck or git log --walk-reflogs to locate them.

data.title: Finding Orphaned Commits
data.code: git fsck --full --no-reflogs | grep commit

data.text: Over time, reflog accumulates stale entries. You can expire reflog entries manually or let Git handle it automatically. A clean reflog makes it easier to find the commit you actually want.

data.title: Expiring Reflog Entries
data.code:
# Expire entries older than 14 days immediately
git reflog expire --expire=14.days --all

# Run garbage collection
git reflog delete --rewrite HEAD@{10}

items: Commit frequently so work is preserved in the object database
Push branches to a remote for off-site backup
Use git stash for uncommitted work before switching branches
Avoid git reset --hard unless you are certain
Tag important milestones so they are easy to find

data.title: Pushing for Backup
data.code: git push origin feature/auth --set-upstream

data.text: When a team member loses commits, they can share their reflog output with a lead. The lead helps identify the correct commit hash and instructs the developer on how to restore it.

items: Share reflog output in a support ticket or Slack thread
Identify the commit hash from the reflog description
Create a recovery branch at the identified commit
Push the recovery branch to origin for collaboration
Investigate the root cause to prevent recurrence

data.title: Team Recovery Request
data.code:
## Lost Commit Recovery Request

### Reporter
@developer
### Lost Commit Description
"fix(auth): handle expired refresh tokens"
### Approximate Date
2026-09-20

### Recovery Steps
1. Run git reflog
2. Identify commit hash
3. Create recovery branch
4. Push to origin

data.text: Reflog is useful for auditing repository activity. You can see when branches were created, deleted, or moved. This is helpful during incident response.

data.title: Auditing Recent Activity
data.code: git reflog | head -20

data.text: CI environments typically do not have meaningful reflogs because they perform fresh clones. For recovery in CI, rely on fetched tags, fetched branches, and commit hashes passed as parameters.

data.title: Tag CI Builds
data.text: Tag CI builds with the commit SHA so you can always return to the exact source state, even if branches move.
Reflog is Git's built-in safety net. It records every reference update, making it possible to recover from accidental deletions, bad resets, and failed rebases.

data.title: Key Takeaways
text: Use git reflog to view reference update history
Recover lost branches or commits by recreating them at the reflog entry
Reflog entries expire; act quickly after a mistake
Push frequently to remote as a backup strategy
